arrow_upward 2.3 Example: Measuring the strength of evidence

2.4 Supplemental Exploration: Measuring the strength of evidence

Tasting water

People spend a lot of money on bottled water. But do they really prefer bottled water to ordinary tap water? Researchers at Longwood University (Lunsford and Dowling Fink, 2010) investigated this question by presenting people who came to a booth at a local festival with four cups of water. Three cups contained different brands of bottled water, and one cup was filled with tap water. Each subject (person) was asked which of the four cups of water they most preferred. Researchers kept track of how many people chose bottled water in order to see whether bottled water was chosen significantly more often than would be expected by random chance.

Step 1: Ask a research question:

participation activity
2.4.1: Question 1.

What is the research question that the researchers hoped to answer?

Step 2: Design a study and collect data:

participation activity

participation activity
2.4.3: Question 3.

Identify the variable. Is the variable quantitative or categorical?

Definition.

A binary variable is a categorical variable with only two outcomes. Often we convert categorical variables with more than two outcomes (e.g., four brands of water) into binary variables (e.g., tap water or not). In this case we also define one outcome to be a “success” and one to be a “failure.”

participation activity

Write this as a binary variable.

participation activity
2.4.5: Question 5.

Describe the parameter of interest (in words). (Hint: The parameter is the long-run proportion of …?)

participation activity
2.4.6: Question 6.

One possibility here is that subjects have an equal preference among all four waters and so are essentially selecting one of the four cups at random. In this case what is the long-run proportion (i.e., probability) that a subject in this study would select bottled water?

participation activity
2.4.7: Question 7.

Another possibility is that the subjects are more likely to prefer bottled water than the tap water. In this case what can you say about the long-run proportion that a subject in this study would select bottled water? (Hint: You are not to specify a particular value this time; instead indicate a direction from a particular value.)

Definition.
  • Null hypothesis typically states the "by-random-chance-alone" explanation, which is used to create the chance model, also called the null model. A null hypothesis is expressed symbolically as H0.
  • Alternative hypothesis typically states the "an-effect-exists" explanation that contradicts the null hypothesis. An alternative hypothesis is expressed symbolically as Ha .
participation activity
2.4.8: Question 8.

Your answers to #6 and #7 should be the null and alternative hypotheses for this study. Which is which?

Step 3: Explore the data:

participation activity
2.4.9: Question 9.

Researchers found that 24 of the 27 subjects selected bottled water. Calculate the value of the relevant statistic.

Use of symbols

Mathematical symbols can be used to represent quantities and simplify your writing. The Greek letter \pi (pronounced "pie") is used to represent a parameter that is a long-run proportion, such as the probability that a (future) subject in this study would choose bottled water as most preferred. The symbol p^ (pronounced "p-hat") is used to represent a statistic that is the proportion of "successes" in a sample, such as the proportion of subjects in this study who did choose bottled water as the most preferred. The symbol n is used to represent the sample size.

participation activity
2.4.10: Question 10.

What is the value of p̂ in this study?

participation activity
2.4.11: Question 11.

What is the value of n in this study?

participation activity
2.4.12: Question 12.

Hypotheses are always conjectures about the unknown parameter \pi. You can also use H0 and HA as short-hand notation for the null and alternative hypotheses, respectively. A colon ":" is used to represent the word "is". Restate the null and alternative hypotheses using \pi.

Step 4: Draw inferences:

participation activity
2.4.13: Question 13.

Is the sample proportion who selected bottled water in this study more than the probability specified in the null hypothesis?

participation activity
2.4.14: Question 14.

Is it possible that this proportion could turn out to be this large even if the null hypothesis was true (i.e., even if people did not really prefer bottled water and were essentially selecting at random from among the four cups)?

As we did with Buzz and Doris previously,, we will use simulation to investigate how surprising the observed sample result (24 of 27 selecting bottled water) would be if in fact subjects did not prefer bottled water and so each had a 3/4 probability of selecting bottled water. (Note also that our null model assumes the same probability for all subjects.)

Think About It.

Can we use a coin to represent the chance model specified by the null hypothesis like before? If not, can you suggest a different random device we could use? What needs to be different about our simulation this time?

We will now use the One Proportion applet to conduct this simulation analysis. Notice that the applet will show us what it would be like if we were simulating with spinners.

2.4.22: Question 18f.

Now enter 995 for the number of samples and click on Draw Samples, bringing the number of simulated samples to 1,000. Comment on the center, variability, and shape of the resulting distribution of sample proportions.

This distribution of simulated sample proportions is called the null distribution, because it is based on assuming the null hypothesis to be true.

participation activity
2.4.23: Question 19.

Recall that the observed value of the sample proportion who selected bottled water in this study was p̂ = 24/27 ≈ 0.8889. Looking at the null distribution you have simulated, is this a very unlikely result when the null hypothesis is true? In other words, is this value far in the tail of the null distribution?

You might very well find that #19 is a bit of a tough call. The value 0.8889 is not far in the tail of the distribution, but it’s also not near the middle of the distribution. To help make a judgment about strength of evidence in this case, we can count how many (and what proportion) of the simulated sample proportions are as extreme or more extreme than the observed value.

participation activity
2.4.24: Question 20.

Use the applet to count how many (and what proportion) of the simulated sample proportions are as or more extreme than the observed value. Make sure that the ≥ inequality symbol is selected (to match the alternative hypothesis). Then enter 0.8889 (the observed sample proportion who chose bottled water) in the box to the left of the Count button. Then click on the Count button. Record the number and proportion of simulated sample proportions that are as extreme or more extreme than the observed value.

Definition.
The p-value is estimated as the proportion of simulated statistics in the null distribution that are at least as extreme (in the direction of the alternative hypothesis) as the value of the statistic actually observed in the research study.

How do we evaluate this p-value as a judgment about strength of evidence provided by the sample data against the null hypothesis? One answer is: The smaller the p-value, the stronger the evidence against the null hypothesis and in favor of the alternative hypothesis. But how small is small enough to regard as convincing? There is no definitive answer, but here are some guidelines:

Table 2.4.1: Guidelines for evaluating strength of evidence from a p-value.
Range Strength of evidence
0.10 < p-value Little to no evidence against the null hypothesis.
0.05 < p-value ≤ 0.10 Moderate evidence against the null hypothesis.
0.01 < p-value ≤ 0.05 Strong evidence against the null hypothesis.
p-value ≤ 0.01 Very strong evidence against the null hypothesis.
participation activity

Exploring further

Instead of focusing on the subjects who chose bottled water, you could instead analyze the data based on the subjects who chose tap water. Because 24 of 27 subjects chose bottled water,we know 3 of the 27 subjects chose tap water. Now let the parameter of interest (denoted by \pi) be the probability that a subject will select tap water as most preferred.

participation activity

Conduct a simulation analysis to assess the strength of evidence provided by the sample Data.

The research conjecture is that subjects tend to select tap water (more or less) often than bottled water.

participation activity
2.4.40: Question 28.

Does your analysis based on the number who chose tap water produce similar conclusions to your previous analysis based on the number who chose bottled water? Explain.

You should have found that it does not matter whether you focus on the number/ proportion that chose tap water or the number/proportion that chose bottled water. In other words, it does not matter which category you define to be a “success” for the preferred water variable. Your findings should be very similar provided that you make the appropriate adjust- ments in your analysis:

  • Using 0.25 instead of 0.75 as the null value of the parameter
  • Changing the alternative hypothesis to “\pi<0.25” rather than “\pi>0.75”
  • Calculating the p-value as the proportion of samples with p^≤0.1111 rather than p^≥0.8889
